This is the same integer program as in Problem 2.  However, in this case, the goal is to solve the problem using cutting planes.
The original integer program is set up for you.  In addition, we have the incumbent solution from the previous problem.
In cutting plane techniques, there often is an incumbent.  But it is not always the case.
All of the cuts are of a special form.  If exactly k variables are positive in an LP solution, and if the sum of their values is greater than k-1, then one can add a "packing constraint".
For example, consider the feasible solution:    "x1 = 0, x2 = 0, x3 = 1                                x4 = 1, x5 = 2/3, x6 = 1"
Since this solution uses all of the budget, there is no feasible solution with                            x3 = x4 = x5 = x6 = 1.
Since all variables of the integer program are binary, we can conclude that                          x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 <= 3
DO NOT include this constraint as part of your LP.  It is just given for illustration.
In this example, all (two) of the packing constraints that you add will be of the form                         "xi + xj + xk <= 2" for some choices if i, j and k.
We  next provide the steps of what we are asking.
Step 1.  Solve the original LP relaxation.
If you conclude from this LP that the incumbent is optimal, then quit.  Otherwise go to Step 2.

Step 2.  Use the solution from the LP for Step 1 to come up with a new packing constraint.  Add this constraint to your LP.  If you did it correctly, then your new LP solution should be different than in Step 1.
If you conclude from this LP that the incumbent is optimal, then quit.  Otherwise go to Step 3.
Step 3.  Use the solution from the LP for Step 2 to come up with a new packing constraint.  Add this constraint to your LP.  Solve the new LP.
If you conclude from this LP that the incumbent is optimal, then say so and quit.  Otherwise say that you cannot conclude that the incumbent is optimal, and quit.
Solving three LPs is enough for you to understand how this approach works.
Incidentally, if you were to try this approach on a very large knapsack (capital budgeting) problem, it runs into an important difficulty.
It's possible that the solution for the LP is not integer, but there is no packing constraint that can be obtained.
That's why cutting plane techniques are typically used as part of branch and bound.  The cuts lead to LPs with better bounds, but they do not typically solve the problem without any branching.
